name: The example
why: 11: a 1-day ticket on day 1 (2), a 7-day pass from day 4 that covers 4, 6, 7 and 8 (7), and a 1-day ticket on day 20 (2).

name: A long pass can be cheaper
why: 2: the 7-day pass costs less than the 1-day ticket, so buy it even for one trip. Try every pass at every step.

name: Far apart
why: 12: three 1-day tickets. No pass covers two of these trips.

name: The last day of a pass
why: 8: a 7-day pass bought on day 1 covers days 1 to 7, not day 8. If you got 5, your pass covers one day too many.

name: Passes in any order
why: 18: a 3-day pass from day 2 and one from day 10 (7 each), and a 1-day ticket on day 40 (4).

name: 100,000 trips in clusters
show: season_tickets(100,000 trips spread over 2 × 10⁹ days, 4 passes)
why: The days go up to about 2,000,000,000, so a table with one entry per calendar day is far too big. Keep one entry per trip, and find the first trip a pass does not cover with binary search (bisect) or a pointer per pass. Memoised recursion fails here: this input needs far more nested calls than Python allows (about 1,000, and only a few hundred with functools.cache in the browser). Fill a table with a loop instead (lesson 3).

name: 100,000 trips in a row
why: Walking forward one trip at a time to find where a pass ends costs up to 100,000 steps per trip with the long pass: about 5 × 10⁹ steps in all. Use binary search, or keep a pointer per pass that only moves forward.
